title: Mark against the class average
allegory: A baseline is like marking each pupil against the class average on the same test instead of against zero: above average earns a nudge up, below average a nudge down, and because the average is the same whichever answer a pupil chose, it doesn't change which answers get encouraged on average, it only removes the noise.
map: a pupil's score on the test
the return G_t that followed an action
the class average on the same test
the baseline b(s_t): ARENA uses the mean return at timestep t across the parallel environments
above or below average: nudge up or nudge down
the sign of G_t − b(s_t), the weight that becomes the advantage
the average is the same whichever answer you chose
b doesn't depend on the action, so E[∇log π(a|s) · b(s)] = 0: no bias
a gold star for everyone vs marking against the average
a high-variance vs a low-variance gradient estimate

cap.1: In CartPole every step you survive pays a point, so every score is positive. Praise each move by its score and good moves look no different from lucky ones.
cap.2: REINFORCE weights ∇log π(a|s) by the return G_t. When every return is positive, every action taken gets pushed up; the only signal left is 'up more' versus 'up less', and one long episode can swamp the batch.
cap.3: With G_t > 0 everywhere, each sample raises the log-probability of whatever action was drawn; the right direction only emerges in expectation, from the relative sizes of the returns, so the estimate is very noisy.

cap.1: A better teacher marks each pupil against the class average on the same test. Above average gets a nudge up, below average a nudge down. Now bad moves get told off.
cap.2: Subtract a baseline from the return: the weight becomes G_t − b(s_t). ARENA's baseline is the mean return at each timestep across the parallel environments, detached from the graph.
cap.3: ψ_t = G_t − b(s_t) with b = returns.mean(dim=0, keepdim=True), detached: a per-timestep mean over environments. Worse-than-average actions now receive negative coefficients.

parts.note: which way to push this action

cap.1: The average is the same whichever move you made, so on average it adds nothing to the push. It can't tilt the answer; it only takes away noise.
cap.2: Because b(s) doesn't depend on the action, it slides out of the expectation: E[∇log π · b(s)] = b(s) · ∇Σ_a π(a|s) = b(s) · ∇1 = 0. Same expected gradient, much less variance.
cap.3: E_{a∼π}[∇_θ log π_θ(a|s)] = Σ_a ∇_θ π_θ(a|s) = ∇_θ 1 = 0, so any action-independent b(s) is an unbiased control variate. Let the 'baseline' depend on the action and the identity no longer holds.

cap.1: Picture many one-batch guesses at the push. Both clouds centre on the same true answer; the baseline pulls the guesses in tight. A sketch, not measured data.
cap.2: Illustrative spread of gradient estimates from single batches: the same mean (unbiased) but a smaller variance, so each update points closer to the true direction and learning is faster and steadier.
cap.3: Unbiasedness pins the mean; the baseline attacks the second moment. A learned state value V(s) is the standard choice, which turns the weight into an advantage; ARENA's per-timestep batch mean is the cheapest useful stand-in.

chapters.name: Sign versus scale

right.title: normalize_returns
lines: step size stops growing with returns

chapters.verdict: Two fixes for two problems: you need both, and keep the 1e-8.

cap.1: Two different fixes. The average gives the sign: better or worse. Rescaling gives the size, so long episodes don't make every nudge huge. You need both.
cap.2: Exercise: normalize_returns is (returns − returns.mean()) / (returns.std() + 1e-8) over all timesteps and trajectories. Keep the 1e-8: a batch with near-zero spread otherwise hands you NaNs.
cap.3: Without normalisation the effective learning rate scales with return size: as CartPole returns grow from about 20 to 500, a setting that was stable early becomes unstable. Keep the weights detached: assert not advantages.requires_grad.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Actor-critic: the critic is the baseline
GRPO: the group's mean is the baseline

cap.1: Every policy-gradient method since grades against a baseline, including the RL that fine-tunes language models. It is how their training signal gets shaped.
cap.2: Swap the batch mean for a learned V(s) and you get actor-critic's advantage. GRPO drops the critic and uses each prompt's group mean and std instead; DeepSeekMath 7B reached 51.7% on MATH that way.
cap.3: PPO's advantage is G − V(s), refined by GAE; GRPO's is (r − mean(r)) / std(r) within one prompt's group, an empirical, critic-free baseline. If a whole group ties, every advantage is zero and that prompt teaches nothing.

coda.title: Slide the baseline, keep the average
labels: push on A if A is drawn
push on A if B is drawn

readouts.label: wobble: spread of a single push

caption.1: Slide the baseline b. The two possible pushes shrink and start to agree, yet the average push never moves. Find the b where all three bars match.
caption.2: A 50/50 policy picks A or B. One REINFORCE sample moves A's logit by 0.5·(r_A − b) or −0.5·(r_B − b). Their average, 0.25·(r_A − r_B), has no b in it: unbiased. The spread shrinks as b nears the mean return.
caption.3: Score-function estimate for θ = logit of A at π(A) = 0.5: ∇log π(A) = 0.5, ∇log π(B) = −0.5. The mean is 0.25(r_A − r_B) for any b; the variance is (r_A + r_B − 2b)²/16, zero at the mean return. Real tasks never reach zero.

where_else: The advantage in actor-critic and PPO: the return minus a learned value baseline V(s)
GRPO's group-relative advantage, which uses each prompt's own group of sampled answers as the baseline instead of a critic
Control variates in Monte Carlo estimation: subtract something whose average you know to cut variance without adding bias

hamming.what: Subtracting a reference value that doesn't depend on the chosen action from the return before it weights the log-probability gradient.
hamming.when: In every policy-gradient method: REINFORCE uses a batch mean, actor-critic and PPO a learned value function, GRPO the mean of a group of sampled answers.
hamming.why: It leaves the expected gradient unchanged but cuts its variance and lets worse-than-usual actions be pushed down, which is what makes policy gradients practical.

object.title: The variance valley
object.subtitle: Height is how much one sampled push wobbles; the true push is the same everywhere on the sheet.
object.f: y*pow(1 - y, 2)*pow(1 + c + gap - x, 2) + (1 - y)*y*y*pow(1 + c - x, 2) - pow(y*(1 - y)*gap, 2)

knobs.label: how much better move A pays

cap.1: Across: the baseline you subtract. Deep: how often the policy picks move A. Height: how much a single-episode push wobbles. The average push is identical everywhere.
cap.2: Two moves with returns r_B = 1 + c and r_A = r_B + gap. Height is the variance of the one-sample REINFORCE gradient for A's logit; its mean, p(1 − p)·gap, has no b in it.
cap.3: Var(b) = p(1−p)²(r_A − b)² + (1−p)p²(r_B − b)² − p²(1−p)²(r_A − r_B)²: a quadratic in b at every p.

cap.1: At zero baseline the wall is high. Walk right and it drops to a floor, then climbs again if you overshoot. Subtracting more is not always better.
cap.2: Too small a baseline and too large a baseline both hurt; the sweet spot sits among the typical returns.
cap.3: The minimum is at b* = (1−p)·r_A + p·r_B, where both outcomes give the same push p(1−p)·gap: zero variance, a special case of two moves with fixed returns.

cap.1: Now pay a bonus on every reward, like CartPole's point per step. The no-baseline wall shoots up, and the valley slides right to follow the rewards.
cap.2: Adding c to every reward leaves the true gradient untouched but grows the no-baseline variance roughly as c². A baseline that tracks the typical return cancels the shift.
cap.3: The offset enters the estimator as c·∇log π(a), zero-mean noise with variance p(1−p)c², which raising b by the same c removes exactly.

cap.1: From above, the valley floor runs at a slant: the best baseline changes with the situation. That is why real baselines are per-state, or learned.
cap.2: The zero-wobble baseline moves as the policy changes, so a fixed number goes stale. ARENA recomputes a per-timestep mean every batch; actor-critic learns V(s).
cap.3: b*(p) = (1−p)r_A + p·r_B drifts with p. A learned V(s) is the standard practical choice; with more actions or random returns the floor lifts above zero.

cap.1: Make both moves pay the same. The true push is zero, yet with no baseline every sample still shoves. Pick the right baseline and every sample says zero.
cap.2: With gap = 0 the true gradient is zero. Without a baseline the samples still shove the logit back and forth; at b = r_B every one of them is zero.
cap.3: With r_A = r_B = r the estimator is ∇log π(a)·(r − b): pure zero-mean noise, silenced exactly at b = r.

predict.q: CartPole pays +1 per step, so every return is positive. With no baseline, what happens to the probability of a bad action you happened to take?

options.t: It goes up, just by less than a good one

predict.why: Every weight is positive, so every sampled action gets pushed up. Only a baseline can hand a bad action a negative weight.

predict.q: You subtract the batch's mean return as a baseline. What happens to the expected gradient?
predict.why: The baseline doesn't depend on which action was taken, so its term averages to zero: E[∇log π · b(s)] = 0. Only the noise changes.

predict.q: Why must a baseline not depend on which action was taken?

options.t: Otherwise it no longer averages out and biases the gradient
Otherwise it is too slow to compute
It should: it ought to reward the chosen action

predict.why: The cancellation E[∇log π(a|s) · b(s)] = 0 works only because b is the same for every action.

object.where: Anywhere a noisy estimate is centred before use: control variates in Monte Carlo, the critic in actor-critic, GRPO's group mean.
